items.prompt: Describe the stages of the program development life cycle, in order.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis states what the program must do, as requirements. Design states how it will do it, as data structures, modules and interfaces. Coding writes it in a language. Testing checks it against the requirements. Maintenance keeps it working after delivery - fixing faults, adapting to a changed environment, improving it for new requirements.
marking_guidance: Order: the stages in sequence - analysis first, then design, coding, testing, maintenance - each statement a mark point, up to 2 from a longer list.
Input: the description starts from the problem as given, with each stage taking the previous stage’s output.
Each statement is a mark point: 1 mark per stage named with its job.
Result: the end product is the whole route from problem to kept-working program, because the stages run in order and each feeds the next.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 12.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how each stage of the life cycle feeds the next.
items.canonical_answer: Each stage’s output is the next stage’s input: the requirements produced in analysis drive the design, the design drives the code written against it, the code is what testing runs and checks against the requirements, and the documented program is what maintenance can change safely, because the stages’ outputs are the chain that links them.
marking_guidance: How the chain works: each stage’s output becomes the next stage’s input - 1 mark.
Because the requirements drive design and design drives code, a fault in an early output travels forwards, so the linking is what makes early stages worth doing well - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A program is written with no testing stage. Explain what happens next.
items.canonical_answer: The untested code goes straight to the users, so every fault the missing stage would have caught - a loop that misses the last item, a total that starts at the wrong value - shows up in use instead, because the faults travel with the code to the users. Each in-use fault costs a user’s wrong result and an emergency fix, which is more expensive than the testing stage it replaced, so the missing stage converts cheap caught faults into expensive live ones.
marking_guidance: Change: the testing stage dropped - 1 mark - so the effect is that the faults reach the users, because nothing checks the code against the requirements.
Consequence: each fault becomes a wrong result and an emergency fix, which costs more than the dropped stage would have, so the result is expensive faults in place of cheap ones - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Describe how the waterfall and the iterative life cycles differ in the way their stages run.
items.canonical_answer: The waterfall runs its stages once, each after the previous and each completed before the next begins, so the program is delivered complete and late. The iterative cycle runs its stages in small repeated passes, each pass delivering a working part of the program, so the program grows part by part and its users see working software early, because the stages loop instead of lining up.
marking_guidance: Order: the stages’ sequence - once through in the waterfall, repeated in passes in the iterative cycle - each statement a mark point.
Input: the description starts from the given two cycles and their stage arrangements.
Each statement is a mark point: the waterfall’s single run in order - 1 mark; the iterative cycle’s repeated passes with a working part each - 1 mark.
Result: the end product is the two shapes of the same stages, because the difference is the arrangement, not the activities.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 12.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how rapid application development compresses the life cycle.
items.canonical_answer: RAD shortens the route from problem to working program by three moves: the users are involved intensively throughout, so the requirements are refined by watching instead of gathered by long analysis; a working prototype is built quickly and reworked, so what users react to is real software rather than a document; and development tools speed the building. The long up-front analysis is traded for a fast first version that users improve, which is how the cycle is compressed.
marking_guidance: How the compression works: prototype-first with the users in the room, so requirements are refined by watching - 1 mark.
Because the fast first version is allowed to be wrong about details and then reworked, the long analysis is traded for immediate reaction, which is the mechanism of the compression - 1 mark.

items.canonical_answer: The answer is true but answers a different question. items.prompt: Explain one benefit of the waterfall life cycle for a fixed-requirement program.
items.canonical_answer: Every stage is completed before the next begins, so the requirements are settled before design, the design before code, and the delivered program is complete and documented. For a fixed-requirement program the single pass is enough, because the requirements will not move underneath the work, and the documentation is what a yearly statutory change arrives to find.
marking_guidance: Benefit: the stages complete in order, delivering a complete documented program - 1 mark.
Because the requirements are fixed, the single pass is not caught out, so the completeness is not paid for in rework - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Explain one drawback of the waterfall life cycle for a program whose users are still discovering what they want.
items.canonical_answer: Nothing works until late: the stages line up once, so the users hold no working software until the end, and their discoveries - the point of watching users, and inevitable while requirements are still forming - arrive after the design and code have been built. A wrong requirement found at testing has travelled through the whole chain, so it is expensive to fix, which is the cost of running one pass over requirements that move.
marking_guidance: Drawback: nothing works until late, so users’ discoveries arrive after the building - 1 mark.
Because a wrong requirement found at testing has already travelled through design and code, late faults are expensive, so the single pass costs more than the requirements’ movement - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A statutory levy calculation is being automated: the rules are fixed in law, and the tax authority wants a complete, documented program. Explain which life cycle suits this work, and why.
items.canonical_answer: The waterfall suits this work. The requirements are fixed and knowable in advance - the law is the requirements document - so the cycle’s demand that requirements be settled first is met for free, and its completeness is what the authority wants: every requirement settled before design, the design before code, and a documented program that a future law change arrives to find. The iterative cycle’s strength - change absorbed pass by pass - would be wasted here, because the requirements will not move, and its risk of a drifted whole is paid for nothing; RAD’s speed is not the priority against documentation. The choice follows the situation: fixed requirements, one complete deliverable, so the waterfall.
marking_guidance: Suitable choice named with the requirements’ situation - 1 mark for the waterfall, because fixed statutory rules meet its demand.
Reason: the completeness and documentation the authority wants are the waterfall’s benefit, so the situation’s priorities name the cycle - 1 mark.
Context: the justification is developed in this scenario - the iterative and RAD strengths are wasted on unmoving requirements, so their risks would be paid for nothing - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A small lodge’s booking program was built with the waterfall, but its owners keep thinking of improvements while seeing the screens, and each improvement waits for the next yearly release. Explain which life cycle would suit this situation better, and why.
items.canonical_answer: The iterative cycle suits it: the stages run in small repeated passes, each pass delivering a working part, so the owners’ improvements - the requirements they discover while watching screens - feed the next pass instead of waiting for a yearly release, because change is that cycle’s normal business. The waterfall’s single pass was built for requirements that stand still, so it queues the owners’ discoveries behind its own shape.

items.prompt: A program built with the iterative cycle is delivered in its first pass, and the users’ reaction reveals that two requirements were misunderstood from the start. Explain what happens next.
items.canonical_answer: The discovery feeds the next pass: the iterative cycle expects requirements to be discovered and changed, so the two misunderstood requirements enter the next pass’s analysis, the design and code of the affected parts are reworked, and the corrected part is delivered again working - which is the cycle’s whole point. The faults were found while they were cheap, in a part built in one small pass, so the correction ripples through a pass and not through a whole single-built program, because the cycle’s shape makes discovery its normal business.

Consequence: the correction costs one pass’s rework instead of a whole program’s, so the discovered faults are cheap, which is what the cycle’s shape buys - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Explain how the three forms of maintenance differ, with one example of each.

items.prompt: A clinic is automating its patient register: the receptionist’s paper register is studied, the doctors’ booking rules are gathered, and the program is then designed, coded, tested and kept working. Write pseudocode for a function NextPatientNumber that takes the array PatientNumbers, of up to 300 INTEGER values with indices 1 to 300, and the count NumPatients, and returns the next patient number to assign - the largest number in the register plus 1, or 1 for an empty register.
items.canonical_answer:
```pseudocode
FUNCTION NextPatientNumber(PatientNumbers : ARRAY[1:300] OF INTEGER, NumPatients : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Largest : INTEGER
   IF NumPatients = 0 THEN
      RETURN 1
   ENDIF
   Largest <- PatientNumbers[1]
   FOR Index <- 2 TO NumPatients
      IF PatientNumbers[Index] > Largest THEN
         Largest <- PatientNumbers[Index]
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Largest + 1
ENDFUNCTION
```
marking_guidance: Mark point 1: the function heading with both parameters and their types, RETURNS INTEGER, and ENDFUNCTION. Mark point 2: the declarations of Index and Largest.
Mark point 3: the initialisation of Largest to the first element, after the empty-register selection. Mark point 4: the selection IF NumPatients = 0 THEN ... ENDIF returning 1 for the empty register.
Mark point 5: the count-controlled loop FOR Index <- 2 TO NumPatients, closed with NEXT Index. Mark point 6: the selection inside the loop comparing PatientNumbers[Index] with Largest.
Mark point 7: the array element read by index throughout. Mark point 8: the value RETURNed at the end - Largest + 1, returned and not output - so the function is complete and closed.

context.situation: A clinic register’s next patient number, coded stage by stage.

items.prompt: A booking program’s maintenance stage: the adaptive change is a new levy of 10 percent on bookings above 500 dollars. Write pseudocode for a function BookingTotal that takes the real BookingAmount and returns the total due - the amount itself, plus 10 percent of the amount when the amount exceeds 500 dollars, and the plain amount otherwise.
items.canonical_answer:
```pseudocode
FUNCTION BookingTotal(BookingAmount : REAL) RETURNS REAL
   DECLARE TotalDue : REAL
   IF BookingAmount > 500 THEN
      TotalDue <- BookingAmount + BookingAmount * 0.1
   ELSE
      TotalDue <- BookingAmount
   ENDIF
   RETURN TotalDue
ENDFUNCTION
```
marking_guidance: Mark point 1: the function heading with the parameter and its type, RETURNS REAL, and ENDFUNCTION. Mark point 2: the declaration of TotalDue, with both branches setting it.
Mark point 3: the selection IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF matching the adaptive rule’s two cases. Mark point 4: the condition BookingAmount > 500, a complete comparison.
Mark point 5: the levy case computing the amount plus 10 percent - the multiplication before the addition. Mark point 6: the else branch carrying the plain amount through.

Mark point 7: the single RETURN at the end, of the variable both branches set, returned and not output. Mark point 8: the function complete and closed - one parameter in, one value back, because the adaptive change is one rule.

context.situation: A levy rule added in the maintenance stage.

items.prompt:
A tax authority is automating a statutory deduction, and a youth centre is building a bookings tool whose young users will keep changing their minds while using early versions.
(a) Explain which life cycle suits the authority’s work and which suits the youth centre’s, with the reason for each. [2]
(b) The authority’s program is delivered, and a fault in the deduction formula is found in the first month of use. Name the form of this change and explain why that form. [2]
(c) The youth centre’s program adds a feature the users asked for after six months. Name the form of this change and explain why that form. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The authority’s statutory work suits the waterfall: the rules are fixed and knowable in advance - the law is the requirements document - so the single pass in stage order is not caught out by moving requirements, and it delivers the completeness and documentation the authority wants. The youth centre’s tool suits the iterative cycle: the requirements are expected to change as the young users watch early versions, so small repeated passes absorb each change while it is cheap, with a working part delivered in every pass.
(b) Corrective maintenance: the change is a fault fix - the formula was wrong from the start, and the fault the testing missed is being repaired, which is what the corrective form is.
(c) Perfective maintenance: the change is a new requirement from the users, improving the delivered program rather than fixing a fault or adapting to a new environment, which is what the perfective form is.
marking_guidance: Part (a): the context of the two given programs - 2 marks, 1 per point: the waterfall for fixed statutory rules, the iterative cycle for users still discovering requirements.
Part (b): the reason for the form - 2 marks, 1 per point: corrective named, because a missed fault being fixed is the corrective reason.
Part (c): the reason for the form - 2 marks, 1 per point: perfective named, because a user-requested improvement is the perfective reason.

context.situation: A statutory deduction and a bookings tool, each on its own cycle.
